what_it_does: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) learn by passing information between connected nodes in a graph — useful for tasks like fraud detection or drug discovery where relationships matter. When GNNs are deployed on edge devices (phones, embedded hardware), both the trained model's weights and the private graph data it processes are at risk of being stolen or reverse-engineered. GNNVault addresses this by splitting the GNN into two parts: a general-purpose backbone that handles most of the computation, and a small private component called a rectifier that fine-tunes the output. Both parts run inside Intel SGX, a hardware feature that creates a walled-off, encrypted region of memory called a Trusted Execution Environment where even the operating system cannot read the data. By keeping the sensitive rectifier and graph data inside this protected enclave, the system shields intellectual property and user privacy without requiring the entire large model to live in the (limited) secure region.
